questions.prompt: The Kubo formula expresses the linear response through
choices: an equal-time expectation value in the perturbed state
a retarded commutator correlation function in the unperturbed equilibrium state, $-i\theta(t-t')\langle[\hat A(t),\hat H'(t')]\rangle_0$
a time-ordered product in the perturbed state
an anticommutator of the unperturbed Hamiltonian with the observable
questions.solution: Eq. (6.8). The average is over the unperturbed equilibrium state, and the time dependence of the states is hidden in the commutator. The other options are not the Kubo form.

questions.prompt: Why does a convolution in time become a product in frequency? And why is the transform of the retarded function defined with $\omega+i\eta$?
questions.solution:
The retarded function depends only on the time difference, Eq. (6.10), so $\delta\langle A\rangle(t)$ is a convolution in time, Eq. (6.11). The convolution theorem turns it into the product $C^R_{AB}(\omega)f(\omega)$, Eq. (6.12).

The response function does not decay in general, so the transform needs the convergence factor $e^{-\eta t}$ in Eq. (5.46). This is the $\omega\to\omega+i\eta$ prescription used for all retarded functions.

questions.prompt: Name the two terms in the Kubo conductivity and where each comes from.
questions.solution:
The conductivity, Eq. (6.24), has two terms:

1. The paramagnetic term $\frac{ie^2}{\omega}\Pi^R$, a retarded current-current correlation function. It comes from the response of the equilibrium current $\hat J$ to the external vector potential.
2. The diamagnetic term $\frac{ie^2n}{\omega m}\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')$. It comes from the explicit $A$-dependence of the current operator, Eq. (1.98c), which is linear in $A$ and contributes without any correlation function.

questions.prompt: For a translation-invariant system, the inverse dielectric function $\varepsilon^{-1}(q,\omega)$ equals
questions.solution: Eq. (6.42). The sign is positive because $\phi_{tot}=\phi_{ext}+\phi_{ind}$ and $\phi_{ind}=V_c\,\rho_{ind}=V_c\chi^R\phi_{ext}$ (Eqs. 6.38-6.39). The response $\chi^R$ itself is negative at low frequency, which makes $\varepsilon^{-1}<1$ (screening). The option $1/(1+\chi^R)$ is not the form, because the inverse dielectric function is linear in $\chi^R$.

questions.prompt: For a translation- and rotation-invariant system, relate $\sigma(q,\omega)$ to the current-current correlation function of $\hat J(q)$ (Book Exercise 6.3).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 6.3. With isotropy, $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\sigma(\mathbf r-\mathbf r')$. Fourier transform in $\mathbf r-\mathbf r'$ and write $\hat{\mathbf J}(\mathbf q)=\int d\mathbf r\,e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}\hat{\mathbf J}(\mathbf r)$. Then Eq. (6.24) gives
$$\sigma(\mathbf q,\omega)=\frac{ie^2}{\omega}\left[\frac{1}{\mathcal V}\,C^R_{J_\alpha(\mathbf q)J_\alpha(-\mathbf q)}(\omega)+\frac{n}{m}\right].$$
The factor $1/\mathcal V$ comes from the normalization of the translation-invariant correlation function (the sum over the volume). The diamagnetic term is $q$-independent and gives the constant $n/m$.

This is the $q$-space version of Eq. (6.24). It shows that the dc conductivity is set by the current-current correlation at momentum $\mathbf q$, plus the diamagnetic constant.

questions.prompt: Non-interacting gas at $q\to0$: derive the current operator, check its time dependence, and find the conductivity. Then discuss the interacting translation-invariant case (Book Exercise 6.4 parts a, b and d; part c, the Drude comparison, is not used here).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 6.4. (a) For free electrons the velocity is $\mathbf v_k=\mathbf k/m$. Taking $q\to0$ in the current operator gives
$$\hat{\mathbf J}(0)=\frac1m\sum_{k\sigma}\mathbf k\,c^\dagger_{k\sigma}c_{k\sigma}.$$

(b) The operator $\hat{\mathbf J}(0)$ is diagonal in $k$, like $H_0=\sum_k\varepsilon_kc^\dagger_kc_k$. Hence $[H_0,\hat{\mathbf J}(0)]=0$ and $\hat{\mathbf J}(0,t)=\hat{\mathbf J}(0)$. The retarded correlation function is then time-independent with zero commutator, so $\Pi^R(0,\omega)=0$. Eq. (6.24) gives
$$\sigma(0,\omega)=\frac{ie^2n}{m\omega}.$$

Dissipative part: with $\omega\to\omega+i\eta$, $\frac{i}{\omega+i\eta}=\mathcal P\frac{i}{\omega}+\pi\delta(\omega)$, so
$$\mathrm{Re}\,\sigma(0,\omega)=\frac{\pi e^2n}{m}\,\delta(\omega).$$
There is no absorption at finite frequency: the electrons accelerate freely.

(d) With interactions, the total momentum $\mathbf P=\sum_k\mathbf k\,n_k$ still commutes with $H$, because the interaction depends only on differences of positions. So $\hat{\mathbf J}(0)=\mathbf P/m$ commutes with $H$ and the same results follow: $\Pi^R(0,\omega)=0$ and the $\delta(\omega)$ weight is $\pi e^2n/m$. The conclusion does not change at $q=0$.

questions.prompt: Show the symmetry $G(\xi,\xi',\omega)=G(\xi',\xi,\omega)$ of the dc conductance function (the Lehmann argument of Book Exercise 6.5).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 6.5. Insert eigenstates of $H_0$ with weights $\rho_n=e^{-\beta E_n}/Z$ into the time-domain function $-i\theta(t)\langle[\hat A(t),\hat B]\rangle$ and Fourier transform. The time integral gives the Lehmann representation
$$C^R_{AB}(\omega)=\sum_{nn'}\frac{(\rho_n-\rho_{n'})\,A_{nn'}B_{n'n}}{\omega+E_n-E_{n'}+i\eta},\qquad A_{nn'}=\langle n|A|n'\rangle.$$

Use $1/(x+i\eta)=\mathcal P(1/x)-i\pi\delta(x)$. The delta-function (absorptive) part is
$$-\pi\sum_{nn'}(\rho_n-\rho_{n'})A_{nn'}B_{n'n}\,\delta(\omega+E_n-E_{n'})=-\tfrac12\int dt\,e^{i\omega t}\langle[A(t),B(0)]\rangle,$$
which is the identity of part (a). It is the part that sets the dc dissipation and is the quantity entering $G$ in the book's hint. With $A=\hat I(\xi)$ and $B=\hat I(\xi')$ this gives
$$G(\xi,\xi',\omega)=\frac{e^2}{2\omega}\int dt\,e^{i\omega t}\langle[\hat I(\xi,t),\hat I(\xi',0)]\rangle.$$

Part (b). Time-translation invariance of the equilibrium average gives $\langle[A(t),B(0)]\rangle=\langle[A(0),B(-t)]\rangle=-\langle[B(-t),A(0)]\rangle$. Substituting $t\to-t$,
$$G_{AB}(\omega)=-\frac{e^2}{2\omega}\int dt\,e^{-i\omega t}\langle[B(t),A(0)]\rangle=G_{BA}(-\omega).$$
At $\omega\to0$ the limit is the derivative, $G_{AB}(0)=\frac{ie^2}{2}\int dt\,t\,\langle[A(t),B(0)]\rangle$. The same substitution shows this integral is unchanged under $A\leftrightarrow B$, so $G(\xi,\xi',0)=G(\xi',\xi,0)$.

Only the dc limit is shown, which is what the book needs.
